The 64-wide subgroup-matrix column tile computes ceilDiv(N, 64) * 64 columns: its trailing tile reads column N - 1 in place of every column at or past N and drops those stores, so a wrong clamp or a missing store guard shows up as a wrong last column or a write past the output. N = 64 + 1 leaves a single live column in the trailing tile, the narrowest tail the guard has to keep.

The 64-wide subgroup-matrix column tile computes ceilDiv(N, 64) * 64 columns: its trailing tile reads column N - 1 in place of every column at or past N and drops those stores, so a wrong clamp or a missing store guard shows up as a wrong last column or a write past the output. N = 64 + 32 splits the trailing tile exactly down the middle of its two 32-column subtiles, so only one subgroup's stores survive.

The 64-wide subgroup-matrix column tile computes ceilDiv(N, 64) * 64 columns: its trailing tile reads column N - 1 in place of every column at or past N and drops those stores, so a wrong clamp or a missing store guard shows up as a wrong last column or a write past the output. N = 64 + 63 leaves one dead column in the trailing tile, the widest tail the guard has to drop.

The 64-wide subgroup-matrix column tile computes ceilDiv(N, 64) * 64 columns: its trailing tile reads column N - 1 in place of every column at or past N and drops those stores, so a wrong clamp or a missing store guard shows up as a wrong last column or a write past the output. A split-K launch writes float32 partials through the same guarded store, so an unguarded column would corrupt the next split's partial block rather than the output.
